question: Is it correct to call Masjid al-Aqsa the third haram?
asked: She grew up hearing that al-Aqsa is the third haram, but she was once corrected and told that it is not a haram, which confused her.
answer:
This is actually a very interesting point, and I'm going to have to summarize it because it is a little bit technical. In order to answer this question, we have to go into a little bit of a tangent: what is a haram, and which harams do we have?

The word *ḥaram* comes from the same root as *ḥarām*. And ḥarām means you don't do something; you're not allowed to do something. And in Islamic law, there are places on earth that are called haram because certain things that are halal outside of this area become ḥarām inside the area. So the term haram means extra holy or extra sacred, because that which might be permissible outside becomes ḥarām inside. So that's why a haram is called haram.

Now, I'm not going to go into too many technicalities for the purposes of this Q&A. Let me say: the vast majority of scholars say that there are two harams in Islam. Pause here, footnote: the Ummah has agreed that Makkah is a haram. One of the four madhhabs says that Medina is blessed and holy, but it's not a haram. But this is an incorrect opinion. The other three madhhabs and the majority of the 'ulama, and the perception that the people have: Medina is also a haram. So we're going to just go with this.

So, to continue: there are two harams without a doubt, Mecca and Medina. And this means certain things are prohibited inside Mecca and Medina that are allowed outside of Mecca and Medina. Also, by unanimous consensus of all the scholars of Islam, the haram of Mecca has more laws, and it is more stringent than the haram of Medina. So in the haram of Mecca there's a long list of things you cannot do. In Medina, the list is shorter and the penalties are less. So Medina is also a haram, but it is not at that level in terms of the laws. I'm not talking about blessings; that's a key point here. When we say haram, it's a legal, technical definition. What it means is that certain things are not allowed in the haram that are allowed outside the haram.

And let me give you some examples. By the way, Allah mentions in the Qur'an: "Did they see that We made the Haram a safe place?" And Allah Himself says in the Qur'an:

> سُبْحَانَ الَّذِي أَسْرَىٰ بِعَبْدِهِ لَيْلًا مِّنَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ إِلَى الْمَسْجِدِ الْأَقْصَى

He calls Makkah Masjid al-Haram, and all of Mecca is Masjid al-Haram. By the way, it's not just the Ka'bah; Mecca is Masjid al-Haram. Just like we said, Masjid al-Aqsa isn't just that one temple or one rock or whatnot; it is the entire region.

So what is not allowed inside of Mecca that is allowed outside of Mecca? Well, first and foremost, according to many scholars (and this is an opinion; there's a controversy in this as well), you must enter the Haram in the state of ihram. And again, the same concept: ihram. You are called muhrim, in ihram, because certain things are not allowed in the state of ihram that are allowed outside; for example, trimming your nails and your hair and whatnot.

Also, of the things that are not allowed in the haram is to harm or to capture anybody, even if they deserve to be captured. Anybody who commits a crime, you are allowed to call the police; the police can go and arrest this criminal and take him to jail. As for the haram of Makkah: if a murderer commits a murder anywhere in the world, and then he flees and runs to Makkah, in Makkah you cannot touch him. In Makkah he is free, because Allah says in the Qur'an: whoever enters it shall be considered safe. So technically, in Islamic law, no matter what crime a person has done outside of Mecca, if they come inside Mecca, then they are protected.

Now, the only exception: if they have done the crime inside Mecca, then they have lost the sanctity of Mecca. Criminals of Mecca are punished in Mecca, yes. But criminals from outside of Mecca, if they turn to Mecca (and by the way, why would they come to Mecca? To repent to Allah, to come closer to Allah), in that case, we cannot touch them. We leave their affair to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala.

Also, in Mecca we cannot touch any natural vegetation, and we cannot hunt any animals. Once upon a time there were gazelles and deer in the desert; there were these antelopes and whatnot in Mecca. By the way, this is not the case anymore; in Arabia, all of these gazelles and wildlife are basically gone. But once upon a time there were deer. In fact, there were even, believe it or not, zebras in the Arabian Peninsula. There were actual zebras in the Arabian Peninsula in the time of the Prophet ﷺ. And so these animals would be hunted, and obviously hunting these animals is what you do to live and to eat. In Mecca, you could not hunt. If the gazelle was wandering, you cannot hunt it. No one is allowed to hunt animals in Mecca.

Even natural vegetation, plants that are coming up: you are not allowed to just pluck that plant if it's natural. If it is a farmer who harvested it and he wants to take the fruits, that is permissible. But somebody who sees a natural plant, a tree that is growing there, cannot touch it as an outsider, as a visitor. Now, the scholars say that if the municipality needs to build a road or whatnot, that's something separate. But you cannot, for no reason, touch an animal or even a tree. All wildlife and all animals are protected inside of the haram, unless of course it is something that will harm you. So if there is a scorpion, you're going to kill the scorpion, or a dangerous snake. Otherwise, you do not touch any animal over there.

Also, of the interesting points of the haram of Mecca is that if a person sees a lost item, something that doesn't belong to him, he is not allowed to touch it. So you see somebody's wallet: you cannot touch that wallet; you leave it there. Some 'ulama have said that if there is a lost and found, you give it to them, and others have said no, you just leave it there and leave it for the lost and found staff to find. You cannot touch a lost item over there. So you have a lot of different rulings as well.

And another ruling: you cannot carry weapons inside of the haram. Now again, this is for non-security; the average person cannot carry weapons in the haram. Also, of course, anybody who intends harm in the haram, the penalty has been made greater for him.

By the way, an interesting point here: the majority of early scholars said (now, this is an opinion that has been abandoned, and even in early Islam there was one madhhab that allowed it) that one cannot rent any land or any property, and it cannot even be sold, because it is an endowment, a waqf from Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. And if we follow this opinion, then life would be very difficult for people, because then how would they live? So because of this, the reality is that a minority position has become the majority, and that's how people live. Because how are you going to... you're not going to rent a room, you're not going to rent somebody's apartment or hotel to live in when you go there? But there was an opinion in early Islam, which was actually the majority opinion, that Mecca is so holy there should not be buying and selling of the property or of the land, or even renting of it. But that is a position that we cannot follow, and as we said, one of the madhhabs of the past allowed it, and that has become the standard.

Now, this is the haram of Mecca. As for the haram of Medina, as we said, it is also sacred, but to a lesser degree. And there's no time to get into the technicalities of why or how that is the case; we're not really interested in that issue. For example, there's no penalty for hunting animals in Medina, but there is a penalty for hunting animals in Mecca. Also, the vegetation in Medina is not sacred compared to the vegetation of Mecca; you can pluck the vegetation of Medina. And other things as well: you don't enter Medina in the state of ihram. So you have a number of differences between Mecca and Medina. But still, Medina is a haram, and it is considered to be a sanctuary, and it is safe, and the Dajjal will not enter either Mecca or Medina. So all of this is there and valid.

Now, how about Jerusalem? How about Jerusalem? Technically speaking (and please listen to me entirely), **Jerusalem is not a haram in the legal sense.** What this means is that there is nothing that is forbidden in Jerusalem that is allowed outside of Jerusalem. You can hunt the animals, you can pluck the trees; other things are allowed. So Jerusalem does not have the technical haram definition that Makkah and Medina do.

Now, this has nothing to do with the sanctity or the blessedness or the barakah of Jerusalem. That's the key point here. Barakah is not the same as haram status, and barakah is broader than haram. Every haram is blessed; there are blessed areas that are not harams. Simple. And Jerusalem is mubarak, but it is not technically a haram, and that is because, as we said, there are no special laws in Jerusalem that allow things or prohibit things that are not allowed outside.

And therefore, regarding the common phrase that Masjid al-Aqsa is thalith al-haramayn, the third of the two harams: if they mean by this that it is a blessed land, then they are right, and Jerusalem is the blessed land. And if they mean that Jerusalem is a technical, legal haram, then we say actually that is not the case.

Ibn Taymiyyah writes, as reported in Majmu' al-Fatawa: there is no haram on earth except for the two harams of Mecca and Medina, and this includes Jerusalem and other lands; they are not harams. Nothing else is called a haram besides Mecca and Medina. And then he says: even if an ignorant person says al-Haram al-Muqaddas and al-Haram al-Khalili, the haram of Ibrahim, these lands are not haram by the ijma' of all the scholars of Islam. The only haram in which there is ijma' is Mecca. And as for Medina, a majority say it is haram, and a minority even say it is not. As I said, there is a difference of opinion, but it is a haram because of a number of hadith about this point. End quote here.

The point being that we differentiate between the term haram in a technical or legal sense and haram in a spiritual sense. And if somebody were to say that al-Aqsa is thalith al-haramayn, and they mean by it sanctified and blessed, inshallah that is not a problem. But if they mean that it is technically and legally a haram, then we should correct this and say: actually, it is not quite that definition, but it is a blessed and a holy land.

Now, this answers the question of our sister. And the fact of the matter is that much more can be said, and I have said much more about the political issues going on these days and what we should do. But I wanted to answer this issue so that we understand that al-Aqsa, Masjid al-Aqsa, is a part of our theology. It is a part of our communal heritage. It is not just a political issue. Yes, there is an element of politics, but for us, Masjid al-Aqsa is also a part of our deen. It is a part of our theology. It is a blessed land, and it has multiple names in the Qur'an, and it has been praised in many different ways in the Qur'an and in the Sunnah. And to travel there and to pray there and to make du'a there and to do khidmah there: all of these are things that we are required to do.

And that is why, all of these hadith about Bayt al-Maqdis and Masjid al-Aqsa: our Prophet ﷺ said them, and Masjid al-Aqsa was not even in the hands of the Muslims. To me, this is a very significant point. Our Prophet ﷺ is talking about the blessings of Bayt al-Maqdis, and Bayt al-Maqdis is under Roman control. And he's talking about traveling to Bayt al-Maqdis, and it is under the control of the Byzantine Empire. What does this demonstrate? That the land and the area is holy for us, and it is our heritage, even if politically others might control it. It is our territory. And our Prophet ﷺ praised it, and the people around it, in so many different narrations.
